title: Vesali is lovely
hook: he looks back at the city turning his whole body, like an elephant, and says how delightful it was (DN 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: dipa. No successor, just the dhamma and your own ground. Your line: be your own island.

The last time you left a place you loved, did you look back? The apartment emptied out, keys on the counter. A hometown in the rearview mirror. A hospital room. Some people can't help it; they turn around at the door. Vesali was a rich, lively city, full of shrines and gardens and a proud, independent people. The Buddha knew it well. It was where the women had walked to ask for ordination, and where a famous courtesan named Ambapali gave him a mango grove and a meal, beating the city's princes to the invitation. In the last months of his life, the old texts show him in Vesali, enjoying it.
screen: `DID YOU LOOK BACK?` → `VESALI, A LIVELY CITY.` → `IN HIS LAST MONTHS, ENJOYING IT.`

segments.voice: Here's a quiet surprise. Sitting at a shrine outside the city one day, the Buddha turns to Ananda and simply names the places he loves. Delightful is Vesali, Ananda. Delightful is this shrine, and that one, and that one, and he lists them by name. An awakened man near the end of his life, enjoying the view. Some people imagine letting go means not caring about anything, being above it all. This moment says something else. He's free of clinging, and he can still say, this place is beautiful. Maybe that's exactly why he can say it so simply, without needing to keep it. Then comes the leaving. After his last alms round in Vesali, as he walks away, he stops and turns to look back at the city. The text says he looked back with the elephant look. The commentary explains the phrase: an elephant doesn't glance over its shoulder; it turns its whole great body to look, and so did he. And he says to Ananda: this is the last time I will look at Vesali. That's all. No speech about impermanence, though he had taught it often. He turns, fully, and looks. Then he turns back and walks on. Two things held together: he loves it, and he lets it go, both completely. Nothing half-turned. One full look at the city, then the road to the next village.
screen: `DELIGHTFUL IS VESALI.` · `FREE OF CLINGING, STILL LOVING.` · `THE ELEPHANT LOOK.` · `THE LAST TIME I'LL SEE IT.` · then, large: `HOW LOVELY IT WAS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place you loved and left, a childhood kitchen, a school, a city, a friend's porch, and walk through it slowly, seeing the light, hearing it. Then, the way an elephant turns, turn your whole attention toward it and say quietly: how lovely it was. Let it be lovely, then let it be past.
Nagapalokita. The elephant look: the Buddha turning his whole body toward Vesali, the places he loved, for one last look.
Your line: how lovely it was. Free of clinging, and still able to call a place delightful. Day eighty, done.

howItsDone: Pilgrims still visit Vaishali in Bihar, India, where an Ashokan pillar and stupa ruins mark places tied to the Buddha's life, and the 'elephant look' is remembered in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, read across Buddhist traditions.

chat.says: If the Buddha let go of clinging, could he still love a place?
options: Yes. He called Vesali delightful, gave it one full last look, and walked on.
No. Letting go meant he no longer cared about any place at all.
Yes, so much that he never wanted to leave Vesali again.
chat.meaning: Free of clinging, he named the places he loved in Vesali, turned his whole body for one last look, and then walked on.
